parole.significato: An area of decayed vegetation (particularly sphagnum moss) which forms a wet spongy ground too soft for walking.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bog (originally chiefly in Ireland and Scotland), from Irish and Scottish Gaelic bogach (“soft, boggy ground”), from Old Irish bog (“soft”), from Proto-Celtic *buggos (“soft, tender”) + Old Irish -ach, from Proto-Celtic *-ākos. parole.significato: A social event with traditional Irish or Scottish music and dancing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish céilí (“Irish dancing session”), Scottish Gaelic ceilidh.
From Irish deoch an dorais and Scottish Gaelic deoch an dorais (“literally, 'door drink'”), from deoch (“a drink”) and dorais (“door”).

parole.significato: A small hill or ridge of hills.
parole.testo: From Irish druim, Scottish Gaelic druim (“back, ridge”).

parole.significato: A division of a poem, especially an epic poem or a Scottish poem; a canto.
parole.testo: From Irish and Scottish Gaelic duan, from Middle Irish dúan, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂p-no- (compare Old Armenian տաւն (tawn, “feast, celebration”), Ancient Greek δαπάνη (dapánē, “cost”), Old Norse tafn (“sacrificial animal”) and Latin damnum (“damage”)), from *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice”).

parole.significato: A seaweed of a reddish-brown color (Palmaria palmata) which is sometimes eaten, as in Scotland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Irish duileasc, Scottish Gaelic duileasg; compare Welsh delysg.

parole.significato: An ancient or medieval fortification; especially a hill-fort in Scotland or Ireland.
parole.testo: From Irish dún or Scottish Gaelic dùn, from Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“fortress”). Cognate with Welsh dinas (“city”). Doublet of town.

parole.significato: A bard, genealogist, or storyteller in Gaelic culture.
parole.testo: From Irish seanchaí and Scottish Gaelic seanchaidh, from Old Irish senchaid.

parole.significato: To realise something; to catch on; to recognize someone or something.
parole.testo: Possibly from Irish and Scottish Gaelic tuig (“to understand”).
Abbreviation of usquebaugh, from Irish uisce beatha (“water of life”) and Scottish Gaelic uisge beatha (“water of life”). Compare whisky and obsolete whiskybae.
